t: Minimum XOR Path in a Grid — DP over Reachable XOR Values
o: Move right/down from corner to corner, minimizing the XOR of visited cells. Values are < 2^10, so every path XOR is an integer in [0, 1023]. Instead of enumerating exponentially many paths, keep, for each cell, the set of achievable XOR values; combining from top and left neighbors takes O(1024) per cell. With m·n ≤ 1000 this is about 1e6 operations.
k: XOR values live in [0, 1023] since grid values < 2^10 — a small, closed domain.
dp[cell] = boolean vector over 1024 values, merged from the top and left predecessors via XOR with grid value.
Answer = smallest achievable value at the bottom-right cell.

a.i: Recursively walk all right/down paths, XORing as you go, and track the minimum at the destination. Exponential in path count (C(m+n-2, m-1)) but fine for tiny grids.
s: At (m-1, n-1), update the global minimum.
a.t: O(C(m+n-2, m-1)) — number of monotone paths, exponential

a.n: Approach 2: DP over the 1024 XOR States
a.i: Process cells in row-major order; each cell inherits the XOR-value sets of its top and left neighbors, XORed with its own value. Booleans over [0, 1024) make each transition linear in the domain size.
s: Maintain prev row and current row of boolean arrays of size 1024.
For each cell, OR in (inherited value XOR grid[i][j]) from top and left.
Answer = min index v with dp[last][v] true.
a.t: O(m·n·1024) — each cell merges two 1024-entry boolean rows
a.sp: O(n·1024) — two rows of boolean arrays

w: The DP over XOR states is the intended solution — the bounded value domain is the whole trick. Pitfalls: seeding the start cell correctly, handling single-row/single-column grids (Example 3), and not confusing 'minimum XOR' with greedy bit choices (XOR paths are not greedy-solvable). Follow-up: maximize instead of minimize (identical code), or count paths achieving the minimum.
